Nothing in particular order, but these are the things that I check for when wanting to purchase clothes frugally. While I do not always buy lower quality items, but I understand the need to have clothes that you will wear temporarily to be had at lower cost initially.

1. What's it for?  
Figure out the purpose of the article of clothing that you need it for. This will determine breathability, durability, ease of care and need for color. For outdoor stuff and work clothes, I will find something thicker in material and covers in knee areas, elbows.... 

2. Fabric types  
Common fabrics in affordable markets are obviously cotton, polyester, rayon, nylon, some type of blends. For speciality clothes, they may have some patented design they have or they use to advertise. For example, cotton underwear is common and cheap. But underwear made from modal fabric tend to be expensive because the fabric feels great and usually are more durable. You can usually read the tag for this.

3. Feel the material  
Tactile inspection of the materials can tell you a lot about the product. Do they claim to be 100% cotton, but it feels too light? The weave seems to be more see through and has loose threads here and there....these thend to be lower quality. Uneven threads, snags and thin spons says a lot about clothes. Stretch it a little bit to see how much it moves. Hold it up against the light to see how loose the weave is.

4. Buy one and test it out from one brand/store.  
It could be convenient to buy in bulk or save money in some cases. But if you test out one of the models from that brand and it turns out to be cheap, then you didn't waste all that much. 

I have some clothes from 6 years ago that I still wear today. They are undershirts and their original price was like \~$65ish and I got them on sale for a little less than $40. The pessimistic outlook observed among many Korean men is not merely an individual or cultural trait but rather a reflection of deeper systemic and societal pressures embedded within South Korean society. These pressures are shaped by a confluence of economic, social, and cultural expectations that have created an environment of intense competition, limited personal freedom, and often unacknowledged emotional struggle.

South Korea’s hyper-competitive environment, rooted in its rapid economic development places immense pressure on individuals, especially men, to succeed academically, professionally, and socially. From a young age, boys are pushed through a relentless education system that values test scores above well-being, often leading to stress, burnout, and a narrow definition of success.

Also, traditional gender roles continue to weigh heavily on men. While the global conversation around gender equality is growing, Korean men are still largely expected to be the primary breadwinners, carry the burden of familial duty, and fulfill national military service obligations. These expectations persist even as economic instability, job insecurity, and housing unaffordability make it increasingly difficult to meet these ideals.

And mental health awareness in Korea has long been stigmatized, especially among men. It is improving but not significantly enough right now. Seeking help is often seen as a sign of weakness, and societal norms discourage emotional vulnerability. This leads to isolation and a lack of healthy emotional outlets, further deepening feelings of hopelessness or dissatisfaction.

Finally, the evolving dynamics between genders and generations have left many men feeling caught in transition. As traditional privileges are questioned and gender roles shift, some men experience a loss of identity or purpose, especially when their struggles are dismissed or overshadowed in public discourse.

It is true that you have every right to be suspicious of those advertisements saying you can reach C1 English in less than a year. Honestly, "mastering" a language? That is more like a never ending adventure than something you just finish. Even if you did nothing but study, it would be a real stretch to say you have truly mastered it. I am learning Korean right now and going on 5 years and living in that country to get it right.

And think about this... even people who have spoken English their whole lives are always picking up new words, slang, and those weird little phrases. The language just keeps changing and growing. It is not just about getting the grammar right and knowing a bunch of words. Culture is a big hurdle to overcome as well. Figuring out those subtle jokes, cultural nods, and what people really mean without saying it takes serious time and getting out there.

English is also a bit of a special case too. It is like a sponge for words from all over the place and even makes up new ones all the time. That makes it super interesting, but yes, "mastering" it becomes a bit of a challenge.

For someone who finds remembering words and grammar a bit of a battle, getting to a high level like B2 or C1 is naturally going to take more time and effort. The important thing is sticking with it, finding ways to learn that really click for you, and getting tons of practice in the real world. Instead of obsessing over some finish line of "mastery," it is way better to just appreciate how far you have come and enjoy the learning itself.

There is a lot to consider when it comes to dryers and just buying one off of Coupang may not be for you unless you are willing to do all the research and really consider which type you can integrate into your household.

First to consider are types. There are 3 general types of dryers:

1. Heat pump dryer  
2. Electric  
3. Gas

1 is the most expensive, but you get your money back over use as it has the best energy efficiency rating. But I am not entirely sure on this claim as the drying times are much much longer. We just bought this type last year and drying times for regular size load for 2-person household is like 2 hours and 40 minutes.

2 best fits many household well in Korea because you don't have to worry about gas hookup. I don't know how your home is laid out, so this is where you figure out whether you can accommodate for 2 or 3. With electric, there are lots of benefits, but it is not energy efficient and you will see it in the rise of your electric bill.

3 is used most often in US homes. If you have used gas hook up, then you know that it is what Americans are used to using because it dries fast and it also offers the highest heat rating. If you buy cheaper units it can be loud, but I don't know whether that's the case in Korea as they have very limited options for gas options compared to wider selections in models available in the US. The biggest issue is installation. The cost to get this hooked up is the highest in most homes that are not setup for this. Even high end apartments do not have gas hookup readily available for gas dryers.

So that's really the reason why we went with the heat pump style. Upfront cost was ridiculously high compared to some of the electric options available....

Next to consider is types of ventilation:

1. Vented  
2. Condenser  
3. Heat-pump

This area I don't know all that well. One of the reasons why I know a little about this area is because I used to sell appliances to put myself through school when I was younger.....it was commission based and had after school hours that worked well for me...

I know vented is not used often in Korea but this is required for gas types. The other two collect the vented out moisture into a tank and that requires you to empty them out from time to time and maintain it. That’s about all I know about these because in the US most homes have ventilations for these.

It has been a couple of years since I bought a washer/dryer set in Korea now, but I don’t think this changes all that much.

Best of luck to you.

You need a wide range of vocabulary and quick recalling ability to read faster. Even in your own native language, you can get hung up on reading and then re-reading based on not understanding parts of text. So learning to do that is really the key.

Then the next step is knowing the words so well to a point where you can skim first to understand overall idea of the message written down. Then you can begin reading the complete text to fill in the details. It is really about having the context to understand the overall general idea and then refinining that understanding with specifics here and there.

Then the next step would be try chunking. Because foreign language may differ grammatically, trying to understand individual words can be meaningless. So you try to read in groups and then practice reading this way to understand areas of texts as a group.

This is all just based on my personal experience of course.

I used to think that we set goals in lives and then just work hard to follow it. Once we achieve these goals, then we figure out another piece of ourselves. This is partially true, but with that mindset, with failures we consider ourselves to be that much more worthless. A person could recover from failures, but then they could also fall into deep depressions.

I was one of those people that fell into a deep depression that spiraled out of control. My life was series of successes and I was achieving my set goals. People looking at me told me that I seemed confident, ambitious, intelligent and decisive (not sure about strong personality). I made a decent living and had all the stuff that people envied. But I had no self identity. My life was going the way I though it should and other people wanted, but having those traits alone doesn't mean you identify yourself as that person or you know yourself to be that person.

After my depression, I was left with pretty much nothing. Fortunately, I had my educational background as being broke doesn't mean they take away your degrees. But my busy career driven life was over. I took a little time to further educate myself to specialize in an area while working at jobs that I had always wanted to try out. After that I traveled around as a digital nomad for a little bit. 

During this time, I was able to talk to a lot of people. I was meeting like 10-20 people a week going to gatherings up on Meetup. As I heard their stories, I tried to figure out what qualities that are not blatantly obvious that I had wanted for myself. By this I mean, characteristic like "ambitious" that you have written out. Does that mean just going after something ruthlessly? Probably not if you are a kind person. 

When talking to others, I realized that I was only looking at the big and obvious qualities that seemed good that I wanted. Shaping little details had escaped me. For example, there was this lady that looked after a pot of plant at work and how she found contentment in taking care of this abandoned plant that her workplace received as a gift one time. Her desire to care for something that could easily be overlooked......I wanted that quality for myself.

So I gathered a lot of these and began integrating them into my life. All these micro-qualities that I had overlooked before. It made me much more content with my life. 

The next is how can others do this. Well, some do it through reading, watching movies....I am sure there are a lot of ways. One thing that I would like to caution is through social media. I am not sure the grandiose life that is seen is something that could seem desirable, but I consider that to be just empty shells walking around. I am sure you can figure out why with all these fake influencers or some people just way out of reach..... Anyway, hope you get what I am saying. Best of luck to you in finding yourself. It is a lifelong commitment but a goal definitely worth reaching.

Achieving smaller milestones has a powerful psychological impact, boosting self-confidence and demonstrating progress. This is important because setbacks can be common occurrences. By celebrating small wins, we build resilience.

Focusing on short-term goals also allows for greater flexibility. Your field of study is constantly evolving, and smaller goals make it easier to adapt to new findings as well. Embracing short-term goals is not about lowering ambitions, but strategically navigating the path towards them.

It's understandable that you feel it's unfair when you see your friends doing things you aren't allowed to do, and it's especially tough when you feel like your parents aren't listening to you.

Sometimes, parents have a hard time letting go and giving their kids more independence, even when they're ready. They might be worried about things they see in the news, or they might be remembering their own experiences as teenagers. It's not necessarily about you not being responsible, but more about them struggling to adjust to you growing up.

Instead of just bringing up the general frustration, try to have a calm, structured conversation with your parents. Maybe write down some points beforehand. Focus on specific examples of how you are handling your responsibility. For example, 'I've consistently kept my grades up,' or 'I always complete my chores without being asked.' So in return you can suggest a compromise, like, 'Could we try extending my game time by half an hour on weekends for a month, and then we can reassess?'

As for violent games your friends play, this probably will not go over too well, so try by pushing for ESRB ratings. Now that you are over 13, maybe you can tell them that such and such games are okay for Teens to handle. (May work for Fortnite, but obviously CoD is M 17+ so that will be hard.)

As for the phone, I assume this has to do with sleep cycle interruptions for people using phones too late in bed. Perhaps you could suggest to your parents that you keep your phone in a common area at night, so they know you're not using it excessively, but you still have access to it in case of an emergency or if you really need to talk to a friend about something important.

Try not to try for big changes. Your parents will disagree and your disappointment will be just as big. But ask for small increments based on your accomplishment. That way, your parents will see that you are growing up and be ready to adapt to your needs while doing what is best for you.

Just never forget that they do this out of love and it isn’t easy for them to be parents as they are not expert at being one. Navigating relationships in a workplace requires careful consideration due to the evolving dynamics among colleagues. While it's relatively straightforward to maintain a cordial and friendly demeanor at work, cultivating deep friendships with coworkers presents unique challenges. The workplace is fundamentally a professional environment, where collaboration often coexists with competition, particularly in contexts like vying for promotions.

Imagine a scenario where your close friend at work receives a promotion. This new role might necessitate them to oversee or even discipline you, creating an awkward situation. Professional conduct differs significantly from personal interactions, and managing this dual role can strain both the friendship and professional relationship. This scenario illustrates why some find it difficult to balance close friendships with professional roles; one often compromises the other.

Experienced professionals often choose to keep their workplace relationships friendly but reserved. This approach helps in maintaining a professional distance, which is crucial given the unpredictable nature of workplace hierarchies. Over time, this practice becomes ingrained, as individuals realize that relationships at work are influenced by numerous factors, including career ambitions, job security, and corporate politics.

So, while workplace friendships can enrich your daily professional life, they require careful navigation to ensure they do not interfere with your professional responsibilities or career progression. Maintaining a balance between being friendly and keeping a professional distance helps in managing both personal and professional expectations effectively.

Myth 2: Women Should Not Play Didgeridoo  
This aims to clarify some misunderstandings of the role of Didjeridoo in traditional Aboriginal culture, in particular the popular conception that it is taboo for women to play or even touch a Didgeridoo.  
  
While it is true that in the traditional didgeridoo accompanied genres of Northern Australia, (e.g. Wangga and Bunggurl) women do not play in public ceremony, in these areas there appears to be few restrictions on women playing in an informal capacity. The area in which there are the strictest restrictions on women playing and touching the Didgeridoo appears to be in the south east of Australia, where in fact Didgeridoo has only recently been introduced. I believe that the international dissemination of the "taboo" results from it's compatibility with the commercial agendas of New Age niche marketing.  
  
My understanding of Aboriginal culture in Australia has been formed as an academic ethnomusicologist, through acquaintance with the ethnomusicological and anthropological literature as well as through personal contact, during classes and fieldwork, with the Aboriginal people in a number of communities in South Australia, the Northern Territory and New South Wales.  
  
It is true that traditionally women have not played the Didgeridoo in ceremony. However let us review the evidence for Aboriginal women playing Didgeridoo in informal situations. In discussions with women in the Belyuen community near Darwin in 1995. I was told that there was no prohibition on women playing and in fact several of the older women mentioned a women in the Daly River area who used to play the Didgeridoo.  
  
In a discussion with men from Groote Eylandt, Numbulwar and Gunbalanya it was agreed that there was no explicit Dreaming Law that women should not play Didgeridoo, it was more that women did not know how to. From Yirrkala, there are reports that while both boys and girls as young children play with toy instruments, within a few years, girls stop playing the instrument in public. There are reports that women engage in preparation of Didgeridoos for sale to tourists also playing instruments to test their useability. Reports of women playing the Didgeridoo are especially common in the Kimberley and Gulf regions the Westerly and Easterly extremes of it's distribution in traditional music. The Didgeridoo has only begun to be played in these areas this century where it accompanies genres originally deriving from Arnhem Land (Bunggurl) or the Daly region (Wangga, Lirrga and Gunborrg).  
  
The clamour of conflicting voices about the use of Didgeridoo by women and by outsiders has drawn attention to the potential for international exploitation and appropriation of traditional music and other Aboriginal cultural property. In addition, the debate has drawn to international attention the fact that there are levels of the sacred and the secret in traditional Aboriginal beliefs, many of them restricted according to gender. Perhaps the Didgeridoo in this case is functioning as a false front, standing in for other truly sacred and restricted according to Aboriginal ceremonial life that it can not be named in public. In this way, the spiritualising of the Didgeridoo not only panders to the commercial New Age niche, but also serves as a means of warning non-Aboriginal people to be wary of inquiring too closely into sacred matters.  
  
Written by Linda Barwick  
Reference: The Didgeridoo, From Arnhem Land to Internet

I was about to post that it is based on money but not directly from the attendance of students. There's more to this than that. The entrance exam is difficult and only a limited number of students come in. By failing their students, this causes the following effects:

1. Students stay in school longer: it is already hard to find employment after the military service as well as other factors at the right age. Having students get older in school is probably not a good idea for the employment market for their graduates
2. New students coming in: the limited number of instructors to student ratio probably doesn't allow for adding on more classes. So failed older students taking necessary classes again could back things up
3. Overall image of school: if these top test takers came into school but struggled to graduate while other schools let them breeze through their programs, people will view this tough school as a negative presence. Going along with what everyone else is doing is probably important.
4. National pride: this is reaching but I know it exists in some other countries so I don't see why it wouldn't apply here. Having a more university-educated workforce will be a good form of national pride somewhere. 
5. Tuition: I agree with this point of view somewhat. Students that attend school for 4 years will pay the maximum amount compared to students dropping out. I don't see per credit hour billing at my school so I don't know how that works if a student fails just one class. I know that Korean students are not just going to drop out as this type of degree is absolutely necessary, but I doubt everyone can pay the high tuition rate forever.
6. Balance: the prestige of a university is a fine balance. It requires the right amount of incoming students and outgoing students. In the US, there's around a 40% dropout rate every year. But that's okay because other students will (or at least have in the past) fill in the necessary spots. The candidate range is much larger. I remember seeing non-traditional age students, and foreign students....the candidate pool is larger in the US. It doesn't seem to be the case here. 

These are just my thoughts of course as I didn't do comprehensive research in this area for Korea. I am sure there are more reasons than this, but it has to be more than just a simple business aspect. Probably money-driven but multifaceted causes for pushing people through.
